ltzf8g: This week you review two classes: what the present perfect is for (**he trabajado**, **has visto**) and how its participles are formed. Here you see it with other examples and in short steps, for studying on your own.
kerxr5: A past that still touches the present
16lp8il: The perfect has two pieces: the present of **haber** (he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han) and a **participle** (_trabajado_, _comido_). Only haber changes; the participle stays the same for every person.
f3mmph: You use it when you look at the past **from today**: with a period that hasn't finished yet (**hoy**, **esta mañana**, **esta semana**, **este año**) or without saying when it happened.
1yey845: The two pieces always go together: _no_ and pronouns go before haber. **No lo he visto**, never _he no visto_ or _he lo visto_.
fq2a6f: The participle in the perfect doesn't change with the person: always **llegado**.
18gjicu: **No** goes before haber; haber and the participle are not separated.
ft087b: **News**: you tell what has happened in a period that is still open. _Hoy he hablado con el jefe._
16dasqi: **Experiences**: you talk about your life up to now, without a date. You ask with **alguna vez** and answer with **nunca**, **una vez**, **dos veces**, **muchas veces**. _¿Has dormido alguna vez en una hamaca? — Nunca._
1aucgqr: **Results**: something happened and you can see it right now. _Se ha ido la luz_ (there's no power). _Me he cortado_ (look at my finger).
z4iu10: If you say **when** it happened in a finished period (_ayer_, _en 2019_, _el lunes pasado_), the perfect doesn't fit: you'll review that next week.
1frz3y5: Do the clock test: if you can add _hasta ahora_ (so far) or _en mi vida_ (in my life), the perfect works.
to2ueo: **Ayer** is a finished period. With the perfect, use an open period, like **hoy**.
tnm65b: In a question about experience you use **alguna vez**; **nunca** is for the negative answer.
1t98sms: Remove the infinitive ending. Verbs in **-ar** take **-ado** (_cantar → cantado_). Verbs in **-er** and **-ir** both take **-ido** (_beber → bebido_, _subir → subido_).
1wnnpnd: When the stem ends in a strong vowel (a, e, o), the i takes an accent: _leer → leído_, _traer → traído_, _oír → oído_, _caer → caído_.
1j19bcg: With haber, the participle doesn't change. But if you use it as an adjective (with **estar** or next to a noun), it does agree: _He cerrado la tienda_ / _La tienda está cerrada_.
7fsc2c: After haber comes the participle: vend**ido**, not the present.
un2lgb: After the **e** of _le-_, the i takes an accent: **leído**.
mw3il6: The irregular forms you'll use most
1d0vfei: Eight very frequent verbs don't follow the rule. Learn them as a family: **abierto**, **escrito**, **puesto**, **visto**, **vuelto**, **roto**, **dicho** and **hecho**.
ibij31: Verbs built on them copy the form: _describir → descrito_, _devolver → devuelto_, _deshacer → deshecho_, _proponer → propuesto_, _descubrir → descubierto_.
zvowuq: A memory trick: five end in **-to** after a consonant (abier**to**, escri**to**, pues**to**, vis**to**, vuel**to**), one in **-to** after a vowel (ro**to**) and two in **-cho** (di**cho**, he**cho**).

1y4kdm8: He, ha and han joined to the participle
1t4i3v5: In spoken sentences, **he**, **ha** and **han** are short words that stick to the participle: _he-hecho_ sounds almost like one word, because the **h** is silent: [eécho].
1rot9zu: If the participle starts with a vowel, the two vowels merge: _ha abierto_ sounds like [abierto] with a slightly long a; _he estado_ sounds like [estado] with a long e. That's why it's easy to confuse _he_ and _ha_: listen carefully to the vowel.
1ksgm1h: **Han** is easy to tell apart thanks to its final **n**, which joins the next vowel: _han ido_ sounds like [a-ni-do].
ma5yi: Even though it's silent, the **h** of haber is always written: _he_, _ha_, _han_. Without h, _a_ is a preposition (_voy a casa_) and _e_ is a conjunction (_padre e hijo_).
nigw2b: The **h** is silent: join _he_ to the participle without a pause.
3pt9i2: The **n** of _han_ moves on to the next vowel: [a-ni-do].
1vlu0mb: _Lo he_ sounds almost like one syllable: [loe].
